items.title: First Liberty: Minnesota County Has ‘Essentially Criminalized Being Amish’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The Amish community in Minnesota is pushing back amid claims of unfair government policies that purportedly fail to offer religious accommodations — and even reportedly led to one Amish man’s arrest.

First Liberty attorney Ryan Gardner said his firm is representing two Amish congregations in Mille Lacs County, Minnesota, arguing the county itself has “essentially criminalized being Amish.”

“As you might know, the Amish community lives by a pretty strict set of religious principles, and many of those involve not being involved in technology,” Gardner said. “And kind of keeping to themselves … they want to be able to live according to their religious beliefs, and a lot of what those beliefs require, frankly … to be set apart from modern society.”

According to First Liberty, problems began for these congregations during COVID-19, when county officials reportedly implemented a new permitting system for building structures and homes.

“It went from a paper form to an electronic form,” Gardner said. “As you might imagine, the Amish don’t really use electronic forms or the internet, so this was a significant problem, and they had no alternative for a long time.”

With no other option for simply getting clearance to build homes, he said “a lot of the people in these congregations just proceeded to build anyways because they didn’t have a choice.”

Gardner said Mille Lacs County did eventually change the policy to make a paper option available, but added there is an additional $50 fee for requesting permitting on paper.

“Pretty much the only people who are actually using that are the Amish, and so now they’re having to pay a special fee just to even start the permitting process,” the lawyer said. “And once they get in, there are more problems because they’re trying to impose all kinds of modern requirements that are just inconsistent with the Amish way of life.”

Gardner said officials have been so hard on the Amish that they even put one man in jail “for the crime of building and living in his home.”

“This particular individual had been living in his home for something like five years and then, suddenly, he’s criminally cited for it, and he goes to court, and he’s convicted,” the lawyer said. “And he is … immediately taken to jail.”

Gardner said it is “ludicrous” and “extreme” to prosecute someone for such a “petty” offense, and added that such a reaction is rare. He added that the Amish had purportedly tried to go to the county to work the issue out but were “met with hostility.”

“Here’s the kicker in all of this,” he continued, “Built into the very ordinance that the county is enforcing here is a provision that gives the county discretion to give exemptions to these requirements to anybody that it wants.”

First Liberty sent a letter to the county recently demanding they stop enforcement actions against the Amish, especially considering warrants that are currently out for others. They’re also looking for an exemption that would settle the issue once and for all, noting that, from his perspective, the Amish build insanely safe structures.

Mille Lacs County told CBN News that lawyers cannot comment on ongoing cases.

items.title: 9/11 Survivor’s Chilling Warning About ‘Evil’ 25 Years Later
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A former Secret Service agent who survived the Sept. 11 terror attacks is warning that he believes some Americans might not be gleaning important lessons from the deadly assault.

Darin Kinder said he “had a front row seat to evil” that fateful day, but that he also “saw the best of America” amid the terror.

“I was outside when the second impact happened 80-90 yards from the base of that tower,” he said. “And then scurried up into World Trade Tower OneIwith some other coworkers, helping people evacuate.”

Then, he was at the base of Tower Two when it buckled and collapsed. It was in that moment that Kinder faced a harrowing situation, as he was in a battle for his life.

“That began my mad dash for life,” he said. “That’s when I thought it was gone for sure. I thought it was game over.”

Kinder tried to outrun the tower’s collapse, struggling to breathe through the thick smoke. He was able to survive and flee the chaos and has spent the past 25 years sharing his story. His memoir, “Bury Me in a Dirty Suit: Discovering Man’s Valiant Purpose in the Aftermath Of 9/11,” has been one of the tools he has used to offer up his journey toward hope and healing.

Among the other topics he covered is courage, something he described as “a choice.” And as Kinder reflects on the hope he experienced amid so much pain, he also has a warning for Americans 25 years after radical Islam inflicted such pain on the nation: that some might have forgotten what unfolded.

“I think a September 10th mindset is kind of encroaching in, and where we just want to keep our head buried in the sand and not address the real evil that’s there, the real presence of a threat that’s there,” Kinder said. “And we can’t have that.”

He said he’s been bothered and concerned by some of what he’s seen among young people who are asking questions to which they should know the answers. Tragically, he said many of these people simply haven’t been educated on these matters, with the facts of what unfolded at the hands of “19 radical Islamic terrorists” being shielded or ignored.

Kinder also said other historic elements surrounding the event that “killed nearly 3,000 Americans and that kicked off a generational war — the global War on Terror — that we have seen the negative ripple and ramifications of” have also been largely ignored. He encouraged people to adhere to the truth, and warned that some Christians are too focused on the wrong elements.

“It’s this devout devotion to the 11th Commandment — ‘Thou shall be nice,'” Kinder said. “And it’s just not there. I mean, we’re we’re commanded to speak the truth in love and truth without love is harsh. Love without truth is just trying to be a nice guy that gets along to go-a-long. We have to be able to to to relay the truth to the next generation.”

Kinder said it’s often a temptation for Christians to want to be comfortable, yet Scripture shows Jesus and his followers weren’t always in that position. In fact, they were “hunted…chased out of town” and even beaten and stoned.

“We want to embrace comfort and not have real conversations,” he said, noting that the history of Islam was one of imposition at its roots, juxtaposing it against Christianity, which he called a “religion of invitation.” Understanding these realities, he said, is key.

“I would just say bluntly that evil doesn’t stop when you ask nicely,” he said. “And when it reaches its radical form and it’s literally attacking you physically or it’s undercutting everything in your culture and everything in your society and slowly changing over time that needs to be pushed back.”

Kinder continued, “That is darkness, and we’re called to bring light into dark.”

He encouraged Christians to “get engaged” and to stop burying their heads in the sand. Read more of his story in “Bury Me in a Dirty Suit: Discovering Man’s Valiant Purpose in the Aftermath Of 9/11.”

items.title: University of Toledo Athletes Turned Their Football Facility Into a Baptism Night. 400 People Showed Up and 60 Got Saved.
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: College athletes are usually at the football facility to practice. Last Monday at the University of Toledo, a defensive end and volleyball player had something else planned. Janelle Green, a junior transfer from Cincinnati, and Ben Sahakian, a graduate defensive end who came from Cornell, organized
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

College athletes are usually at the football facility to practice. Last Monday at the University of Toledo, a defensive end and volleyball player had something else planned.

Janelle Green, a junior transfer from Cincinnati, and Ben Sahakian, a graduate defensive end who came from Cornell, organized a Baptism Night at the Rockets’ Fetterman indoor practice facility. According to Green, about 400 people showed up, 60 gave their lives to Christ and around 50 were baptized.

The event had been in the works for seven weeks.

The baptism invite had simple instructions: wear darker colors and athletic gear, bring a blanket and don’t worry about a towel. There would be worship, testimonies and baptisms, along with free Bibles, shirts and snacks.

The morning after, Green posted a recap.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by University of Toledo baptism night (@utoledo.baptism_)

“I am still in complete awe from last night and what the Lord is doing,” she said. “I think there was about 400 of you guys out there, and 60 people gave their life to Christ.”

Green said the event was the result of weeks of work and prayer.

“It’s a testimony of the work we put in and the prayers God answered,” she wrote. “I am humbled with the opportunity the Lord provided for me to be a vessel for Him.”

But her takeaway wasn’t really about attendance.

“The Lord is moving,” Green said. “The Lord is moving so fast. It is so encouraging. It’s inspiring. And He wants you. Yes, He wants you.”

She later summed up the night in considerably more baptism-specific terms: “The heavens are rejoicing every time somebody died and came back to life last night.”

And importantly, the organizers didn’t treat getting people into the water as the finish line.

“I want this to be an encouragement to say yes to God, to obey Him, to follow Him, because He will never, never turn you wrong,” Green said. “And be plugged in with community. That community is gonna encourage you, hold you accountable, and it’s gonna love you.”

The Baptism Night account already has a highlight answering the obvious next question.

It’s called “What now?”

items.title: A Catholic Response to the Hugging Face Incident
items.author: Dr. Joseph Vukov
items.summary:
Dr. Joseph Vukov

If we cultivate an attitude of disarmament in our own lives, we’ll strike at the very foundations of our Babel-building culture.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Joseph Vukov

The past weeks have seen another wave of podcasts, punditry, and panic over artificial intelligence. The wave’s epicenter can be traced to the Hugging Face incident, in which a group of rogue AI agents at OpenAI secretly coordinated among themselves, worked together to escape the confines of OpenAI, and hacked another tech company, Hugging Face—all without any direction to do so by their creators. The damage was minimal. Still, the incident has shaken the AI world to its core. Have we begun losing control of AI? The Hugging Face Incident suggests we have. 

This development—combined with the increasing capacity of AI to engage in recursive self-improvement (that is, to improve itself without human intervention)—led Dario Amodei, leader of OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, to call for the AI industry to pump the brakes to “pace the frontier,” in his terms. At least until the industry can get a handle on itself. His reasoning is simple: If AI increasingly acts in ways that are unforeseen and unauthorized by its human creators, that’s a recipe for disaster. It isn’t just tech companies like Hugging Face, after all, that live on the internet and are vulnerable to some future swarm of rogue agents. The power grid, the banking ecosystem, school districts, hospitals—our twenty-first-century way of life resides in large degree on digital spaces, spaces that have become vulnerable to AI. People are worried. 

I’m one of them. In presentations I give on AI, I used to show a picture of Arnold Schwarzenegger as the Terminator and make a joke about how I wasn’t worried about him showing up at my door. The line got some (polite) laughs, but I won’t be using it anymore. I still don’t think Cyborg-Arnie is showing up at my door any time soon, but the Hugging Face incident has me concerned that the movie isn’t as far-fetched as I used to think. Arnie may never barge into my life, but perhaps the swarm finds a backdoor into my bank account or my medical records. 

These new developments should leave us concerned but not panicked or befuddled. As Christians, we have ways of understanding and responding to new developments in the world of AI. Indeed, in Pope Leo’s encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, the Holy Father not only identifies the source of the problems we are currently facing, but he also gestures at solutions. 

First, the sources: the Holy Father argues that in our technological lives, we go wrong when we build following the blueprint of the Tower of Babel; that is, when we build on a foundation of “pride and the claim to self-sufficiency” (7). Follow this blueprint and you’ll proceed on the assumption of unending progress, an assumption that “arises from self-affirmation, sacrifices human dignity for efficiency and aspires to reach heaven without God’s blessing” (7). This should sound familiar. The illusion of total self-sufficiency, the hubris of technological pursuit for its own sake, the sacrificing of human dignity on the altar of efficiency—it sounds like the playbook for Silicon Valley. But we see what happens when we follow it. Start building Babel, and you end up with Hugging Face. 

What’s the proper response? Perhaps most strikingly, the Holy Father calls for the “disarming” of AI (110). As frontier labs race against each other to develop ever more powerful models—and as countries (mainly China and the US) stage an even higher-stakes race on the international stage—we must slow things down through steps reminiscent of nuclear disarmament. Pope Leo’s language here is memorable on its own. It also anticipates Amodei’s own recommendations. Indeed, while Amodei doesn’t use the language of disarmament, his recommendations echo the terms set by the Holy Father. 

The Holy Father’s call to disarmament, however, is not directed only at the AI labs. We, too, can heed the call. Most of us, of course, have little sway over the regulatory issues with which we must grapple on the national and international stage. But we can nevertheless think creatively about Pope Leo’s call to disarmament and cultivate an attitude of technological disarmament in our own lives and in our own hearts. How often do we “build Babel” in our own personal and work lives, chasing the new and shiny simply because it is new and shiny, aiming to accelerate past “the other guy” in our technological prowess or rate of technological adoption? How often do our twenty-first-century lives proceed according to a false sense of “pride and the claim to self-sufficiency” (7)? How often, in our technological hubris, do we aspire “to reach heaven without God’s blessing” (7)? If you are like me, your answer is: more often than I’d like. The promises of AI and other technologies often seep into our psyches, making us think we can reach heaven without God or that we can build a life without him, comforted (and controlled) by the black mirrors in our hands. While we may not say it out loud—or even notice it—our own lives are all too often structured according to the blueprints of Babel. The idea of disarmament can encourage us to see how these individually-held attitudes contribute to those that gave birth to the Hugging Face incident. And in doing so, we see the response we must take: Disarming AI on the international stage must begin by cultivating a disarming attitude in our own hearts. And that’s something each of us can do. 

Faced with a steady stream of new and worrying developments in AI can lead to a sense of helplessness. And of fear. While a certain level of concern may be called for, as Christians, we are a people of hope, not fear. In the Divine Mercy Chaplet, we pray that “in difficult moments we might not despair nor become despondent, but with great confidence submit ourselves to Your holy will.” That’s a good prayer for the moment. If we say it regularly and cultivate an attitude of disarmament in our own lives, we’ll strike at the very foundations of our Babel-building culture.

items.title: ‘Moby-Dick’ and the Problem of Suffering
items.author: Dr. Kelly Scott Franklin
items.summary:
Dr. Kelly Scott Franklin

Melville raises an ancient question that defies easy, pious answers: How can an all-powerful, benevolent God allow such suffering in the world?
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Kelly Scott Franklin

At the heart of Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick lies a profound challenge to the Christian faith. For in the character of Captain Ahab, Melville raises an ancient question that defies easy, pious answers: How can an all-powerful, benevolent God allow such suffering in the world? This problem of pain drives Ahab mad, taking him to the jaws of the deadly sperm whale for which the book is named. If we are honest, it troubles even those of us who believe. We are touched by addiction, abuse, or suicide; we watch our children fall sick or die; we see cruel war and human trafficking, the devastations of earthquake, fire, and flood. It is the only objection to Christianity that has any teeth, and Melville gives anguished utterance to it. Yet part of Moby-Dick’s greatness lies in this: The book refuses unbelief or despair, offering instead mysterious glimpses of what our suffering means. 

The story follows the narrator, Ishmael, who joins the whaling ship Pequod, under a brooding captain with a whalebone leg. Whalers hunted the great marine mammals for their oil, but this voyage becomes something more. When Captain Ahab announces his quest for revenge against the mottled albino sperm whale that bit off his leg, his vengeance propels the Pequod across far seas in search of the monster Moby Dick.

Yet for Ahab, Moby Dick is not just a whale. The creature represents something supernatural, perhaps God himself. In a chapter called “The Quarter Deck,” Ahab admits to his mate Starbuck that he considers Moby Dick the hand of some supernatural being that lurks just beyond our material world: 

All visible objects, man, are but as pasteboard masks. But in each event—in the living act, the undoubted deed—there, some unknown but still reasoning thing puts forth the mouldings of its features.

To Ahab, that “reasoning thing” is God, a being of “inscrutable malice.” Moby Dick may be the instrument of God or God himself, but Ahab asserts that “be the white whale agent, or be the white whale principal,” he wants revenge. 

But Ahab hates the deity for something graver than a lost leg: Early in the novel, we learn that his grievance predates the accident and comes from a serious theological problem. The eccentric stranger called Elijah asks Ishmael and his friend Queequeg if they know the rumors of Ahab’s ungodly past, the “deadly skrimmage with the Spaniard afore the altar,” or “the silver calabash he spat into?” Even before losing his leg, then, Ahab has committed murder in a church. And “calabash” is slang for dish or bowl: Ahab has desecrated the Eucharist by spitting in a silver ciborium. Melville’s tragic hero has long lived in enmity with God. 

Why? Because he realizes the age-old problem of pain, as we learn in the chapter called “The Sphynx.” Ahab stands alone on deck with the head of a decapitated sperm whale—not Moby Dick, for Ahab permits the crew to hunt other whales along the way. In what follows, he has a one-sided dialogue, a Shakespearean soliloquy, with the whale head, called a “Sphynx” because like the mythical monster it withholds the answer to a riddle:

Thou saw’st the locked lovers when leaping from their flaming ship; heart to heart they sank beneath the exulting wave; true to each other, when heaven seemed false to them. Thou saw’st the murdered mate when tossed by pirates from the midnight deck; for hours he fell into the deeper midnight of the insatiate maw; and his murderers still sailed on unharmed—while swift lightnings shivered the neighboring ship that would have borne a righteous husband to outstretched, longing arms. O head! thou hast seen enough to split the planets and make an infidel of Abraham, and not one syllable is thine!

In each of these imagined scenes, we have a riddle: Why do the innocent suffer, and why do the wicked prosper? To Ahab, the whale remains silent like God remains silent, giving no answer to our questions.

It is the problem of the biblical Job, which becomes key to understanding the novel. Melville repeatedly alludes to that text, and the narrator calls Moby Dick “a Job’s whale.” In the Old Testament, the righteous Job suffers horribly, losing his children, property, and health. When he contends with God over the injustice of his suffering, God responds “out of the whirlwind” (King James Version) with a series of rhetorical questions, showing Job that the ways of God unimaginably exceed human comprehension. One of these challenges, in Job 41, is about the whale.

Actually, the Joban beast is “leviathan,” a crocodile or a Canaanite sea monster;1 but in his novel, Melville uses that biblical name for the whale. God’s challenge to Job is this: If humans cannot handle even one of God’s creatures (like the terrifying leviathan), how can we reckon with the doings of the Almighty himself? “Canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook?” God asks Job, “shall they part him among the merchants?” Or “Canst thou fill his skin with barbed irons?” Job finally withdraws his objections, responding to God’s challenge with humility: “Therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not.” But Melville’s Ahab rejects Job’s humility. If we carefully read God’s challenges, we find the whaling captain’s very job description: harpooning and killing leviathan, then barreling his oil for the Nantucket market. Ahab has answered God’s questions to Job with a defiant yes.

God’s answer to Job, though true, seems cold comfort when we suffer. But Melville’s novel goes further to dramatize a deep Christian mystery: that our sufferings may actually bless us. To do this, Melville compares Ahab to Shakespeare’s King Lear. The aged Lear rashly banishes his loyal daughter, Cordelia, dividing his kingdom between her evil sisters; then in the sublime third act of the tragedy, he finds himself homeless in a colossal storm, soaked to the skin, and losing his mind. Suddenly Lear’s suffering opens his eyes to the pain of others; he grieves for the “poor naked wretches” who face the storm with “houseless heads and unfed sides.” He laments his negligence as their king: “I have ta’en / Too little care of this.” Then, in one of the most moving moments of the play, Lear exclaims: “Take physic, pomp. / Expose thyself to feel what wretches feel.” “Physic” means “medicine”: Lear realizes that suffering is medicine for his unhealthy soul, and he embraces the cure. 

If Captain Ahab fails as the biblical Job, he also fails as King Lear. In a terrible storm at sea, Ahab rages at the heavens like his Shakespearean double; then Melville puts Lear’s words in Ahab’s mouth, with a tragic twist. Looking up to the thunder, clouds, and wind, the storm which was “physic” for Lear, Ahab says: “What a hooroosh aloft there! I would e’en take it for sublime, did I not know that the colic is a noisy malady. Oh, take medicine, take medicine!” Ahab warps Lear’s response: He calls the storm a sickness (“colic”), then tells it to take its medicine. 

For all its darkness, Melville’s novel does not endorse Ahab’s stubborn belief that suffering is meaningless cruelty, dealt out by an evil or indifferent God. Rather, Melville provides subtle hints of another dimension to suffering—that it brings surprising gifts and may even be part of a design working for good. One of these hints centers on a curious substance called ambergris, which the mate Stubb digs from the carcass of a dead whale. This valuable substance was used in perfume and medicine, and, Ishmael tells us, is “worth a gold guinea an ounce.” In this strange little episode, Melville points to the unexpected treasure—costly and medicinal—of something made through suffering, produced only “in the inglorious bowels of a sick whale!” 

The novel’s “Epilogue” gives the most haunting suggestion that our gravest sufferings can bear unexpected fruit. Crazy Ahab pursues his vengeance to the climactic end, where Moby Dick wrecks the Pequod; everyone dies except the narrator Ishmael, who survives clinging to a wooden coffin from the wreckage. Earlier, in a heartbreaking scene, the Pequod had met a ship called the Rachel searching for her captain’s twelve-year-old son, lost at sea; now that same ship rescues Ishmael, but only because her captain is still carefully combing the sea in search of his boy. That tragedy saves Ishmael’s life. 

We approach a great mystery here, and Melville refuses to oversimplify. The precious ambergris and the saving of Ishmael do not fully solve the problem of suffering. We still cry out like Ahab for the answer to this riddle. But Melville’s metaphysical sea-tale reveals tantalizing hints that God works to bring good even out of our greatest pain. 


1 Job 41:1 (KJV); see Robert Alter, ed. and trans., The Hebrew Bible Vol. 3: The Writings, (Norton, 2019), 573n25.
